descriptionChirho: To bring a formal legal accusation or charge against someone, used across all voices and tenses in NT judicial contexts. All six NT occurrences appear in Luke-Acts and Romans, consistently in legal/forensic settings. Active: 'who will bring a charge against God's elect?' (Rom 8:33, egkalesei future active); the Ephesian town clerk directs complainants to the courts: 'let them accuse one another' (Acts 19:38, egkaleitosan present active imperative); the Jews 'were accusing' Paul before the tribune (Acts 23:28, enekaloun imperfect active). Passive: Paul twice declares 'I am accused' before Agrippa (Acts 26:2, 26:7, egkaloumai present middle/passive); 'being accused' as a participle describing Paul (Acts 23:29, egkaloumenon); 'to be accused of rioting' (Acts 19:40, egkaleisthai present passive infinitive). The semantic core is uniform: formal legal prosecution. All multilingual glosses confirm a single meaning: Arabic uttahamu 'accuse,' Hebrew mu'sham/he'eshimu, Hindi dosh-lagaya, Korean goso-danghaneun/goso-hal, Spanish acusar/ser-acusado.
